results.answer: FY2018 capital expenditure for 3M was $1,577 million, shown as "Purchases of property, plant and equipment (PP&E)" of (1,577) in the 2018 column of the consolidated cash flow statement (up from $1,373M in 2017). This is the cash outflow for PP&E in investing activities.

3M's FY2018 year-end net PP&E was $8.738 billion (USD 8,738 million): gross PP&E of $24,873 million less accumulated depreciation of $16,135 million, as reported on the Consolidated Balance Sheet at December 31, 2018.

Not especially. FY2022 capex was $1,749M on $34,229M net sales, or about 5.1% of sales. Net PP&E of $9,178M is about 19.8% of $46,455M total assets and about 26.8% of sales. That is a moderate asset base for a diversified manufacturer, and the 2022 figures alone give no peer benchmark, so the verdict is a judgment: moderately, not highly, capital-intensive. Ratios are my calculations from the cited figures.

3M's reported operating income margin fell 1.7 points, from 20.8% in 2021 to 19.1% in 2022. Raw material cost inflation was the largest operating drag (-2.4 pts), and net special items cost a further 1.7 pts (PFAS manufacturing exit costs -2.4, Russia exit -0.3, litigation -6.7, partly offset by a +8.0 pt gain on business divestitures). Organic growth, pricing and productivity added +1.0 pt. Operating margin is a useful metric for 3M because the company reports it and bridges it explicitly, but the reported figure is heavily affected by special items, so the bridge to the ex-special-items margin (22.2% in 2022 vs 20.8% in 2021 on the same basis) is needed to read the underlying trend.

Consumer. Excluding M&A (acquisitions were zero in every segment in 2022, and divestitures are excluded by using organic sales), Consumer's organic sales fell 0.9% while total company organic sales rose 1.2%. Consumer was the only segment with negative organic growth; Safety and Industrial grew 1.0%, Transportation and Electronics 1.2%, and Health Care 3.2%.

Not clearly healthy on a quick-ratio basis, though the quick ratio is a relevant measure here. Quick ratio at June 30, 2023 = (cash 4,258 + current marketable securities 56 + receivables 4,947) / current liabilities 10,936 = 9,261 / 10,936 ≈ 0.85x, below the 1.0x benchmark. Justification: the ratio excludes inventories (5,280) and prepaids, and it sits below 1.0x even though 3M's current ratio is about 1.44x (15,754 / 10,936) and it held $4.3B of cash and marketable securities; the balance sheet also shows short-term borrowings rising to 3,033 from 1,938, which is why the cash cushion is thinner than the current ratio suggests.

Three debt securities are registered under 3M's name on the New York Stock Exchange in the Q2 2023 10-Q (quarter ended June 30, 2023): the 1.500% Notes due 2026 (MMM26), the 1.750% Notes due 2030 (MMM30), and the 1.500% Notes due 2031 (MMM31). The cover page's Section 12(b) table lists these three notes, each against New York Stock Exchange; the common stock is the only other class listed there.

Yes. 3M has paid dividends every year since 1916 and has raised its per-share dividend every year in the period shown. Cash dividends paid per share rose from $3.42 (2014) to $4.10 (2015), $4.44 (2016), $4.70 (2017), $5.44 (2018), $5.76 (2019), $5.88 (2020), $5.92 (2021) and $5.96 (2022). Growth slowed from double digits in 2015 and 2018 to about 1% a year in 2021 and 2022. In February 2023 the board declared a first-quarter 2023 dividend of $1.50 per share, up 1%, marking the 65th consecutive year of dividend increases. The payout is stable and steadily growing, though the increases have become small.

FY2019 fixed asset turnover ≈ 24.26x. Total net revenues of $6,489M divided by average net PP&E of $267.5M (($253M + $282M) / 2) gives 24.26. Net PP&E is taken from the consolidated balance sheet and revenue from the consolidated statement of operations.

1.9% — 3-year average of capex/revenue for FY2017–FY2019: FY2017 155/7,017 = 2.21%, FY2018 131/7,500 = 1.75%, FY2019 116/6,489 = 1.79%; average ≈ 1.91%, rounded to 1.9%. Capex is the "Capital expenditures" line of the cash flow statement and revenue is "Total net revenues" from the statement of operations, both in the FY2019 10-K.

Adobe's FY2015 operating cash flow ratio is 0.66: net cash provided by operating activities of $1,469,502K divided by total current liabilities of $2,213,556K (as of November 27, 2015) gives 0.6639, which rounds to 0.66.

Adobe's GAAP operating income rose about 65.4% year over year, from $903,095K in FY2015 to $1,493,602K in FY2016: (1,493,602 − 903,095) / 903,095 = 65.4%. This is the reported, unadjusted operating income line on the consolidated statements of income.

FY2017 operating cash flow ratio = 2,912,853 / 3,527,457 = 0.83. Net cash provided by operating activities was $2,912,853K and total current liabilities at December 1, 2017 were $3,527,457K (both in thousands, Adobe fiscal 2017).

No. Adobe's GAAP operating margin did not improve in FY2022. It fell to 34.6% from 36.8% in FY2021, though it was still above FY2020's 32.9%. Computed from the income statement: operating income $6,098M / total revenue $17,606M = 34.6% (FY2021: $5,802M / $15,785M = 36.8%; FY2020: $4,237M / $12,868M = 32.9%). Operating margin is a meaningful metric for Adobe because it reports GAAP operating income, not a loss-making profile. The FY2022 decline came from operating expenses growing faster than revenue: opex rose to 53.1% of revenue from 51.4%, and gross margin slipped to 87.7% from 88.2%.

Yes, on the usual definition (FCF ÷ net income). FCF = operating cash flow minus purchases of property and equipment: FY2020 $5,308M, FY2021 $6,882M, FY2022 $7,396M. Divided by net income ($5,260M, $4,822M, $4,756M), conversion rose from 100.9% to 142.7% to 155.5%. Caveat: FCF as a share of revenue was roughly flat, 41.3% → 43.6% → 42.0%, and slipped in FY2022. The 10-K does not define a free cash flow metric, so these figures are my calculation from the reported statements.

0. AES Corporation's FY2022 Consolidated Statements of Operations has no restructuring cost line; the lines are revenue, cost of sales, G&A, interest, impairments, goodwill impairment, and other items. The only restructuring mention in the 10-K is a non-GAAP adjustment for the 2018 restructuring program, which is not an income statement line.

About 12 times in FY2022. Using average inventory, turnover = total cost of sales $10,069M ÷ average inventory (($1,055M + $604M) ÷ 2 = $829.5M) ≈ 12.1x, or roughly every 30 days. On year-end inventory alone it is ≈ 9.5x. Conventional turnover is only a rough proxy here: AES's inventory is mainly fuel and other raw materials ($733M) plus spare parts and supplies ($322M), and spare parts are consumed in maintenance rather than sold, while cost of sales is a broad operating cost line, so the ratio is indicative rather than a precise measure of sales of goods.

FY2022 ROA is -1.42% (≈ -0.0142). Net income (loss) of $(505)M divided by average total assets of $35,663M (($38,363M + $32,963M) / 2) gives -505 / 35,663 = -1.42%. The loss is the consolidated net income (loss) line, before the attribution to noncontrolling interests.

FY2017 DPO ≈ 93.86 days. Average accounts payable = (25,309 + 34,616) / 2 = 29,962.5 $M. Denominator = FY2017 cost of sales 111,934 + inventory change (16,047 − 11,461 = 4,586) = 116,520 $M. DPO = 365 × 29,962.5 / 116,520 = 93.86. Accounts payable and inventories come from the balance sheet, and cost of sales from the statement of operations.

Amazon's total net sales rose 30.8% from FY2016 to FY2017: ($177,866M − $135,987M) / $135,987M = 41,879 / 135,987 ≈ 30.8%. Total net sales is the revenue line on the consolidated statement of operations.

USD 11,588 million. The FY2019 income statement reports Net income of $11,588M and has no noncontrolling-interest line, so with no deduction shown, net income attributable to shareholders equals net income.

Amcor's FY2020 year-end net trade receivables were $1,615.9 million (as of June 30, 2020), taken directly from the balance sheet line "Trade receivables, net"; no calculation was needed. The FY2019 comparative was $1,864.3 million.

The 1 July 2022 Amcor plc Form 8-K (Item 8.01 Other Events only) reports that on June 30, 2022 Amcor Finance (USA), Inc. (Former Issuer) and Amcor Flexibles North America, Inc. (Substitute Issuer) signed a Second Supplemental Indenture (to the 2016 Indenture) and a First Supplemental Indenture (to the 2019 Indenture) with Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas, substituting the Substitute Issuer for the Former Issuer and having it assume the Former Issuer's covenants on the 3.625% Guaranteed Senior Notes due 2026 and 4.500% Guaranteed Senior Notes due 2028. The filing's Item 9.01 lists these supplemental indentures as Exhibits 4.6 and 4.7.

Improved. Quick ratio = (cash + trade receivables) / total current liabilities, in $ millions. FY2023: (689 + 1,875) / 4,476 ≈ 0.57x. FY2022: (775 + 1,935) / 5,103 ≈ 0.53x. The ratio rose by about 0.04x, mainly because current liabilities fell from 5,103 to 4,476 while cash and receivables fell less. Quick ratio is a standard liquidity metric, so it is a reasonable question for Amcor. Amcor's quick ratio is below 1.0x in both years, so it depends on inventory and operating cash flow.

FY2023: three acquisitions, all in Flexibles: (1) DGPack s.r.o., a Czech flexible-packaging plant, closed Aug 1, 2022 for $59M; (2) a medical device packaging site in Shanghai, China, closed Mar 17, 2023 for $60M; (3) a New Zealand maker of automated protein packaging machines, closed May 31, 2023 for $45M. FY2022: no acquisitions are disclosed in the FY2022 10-K. Its only portfolio activity was disposals, the Russian business classified as held for sale and non-core Flexibles asset disposals. The April 2022 8-K is a $1.875B revolving credit facility, not an acquisition. FY2021: no new acquisitions are disclosed. The FY2021 10-K's major acquisition is Bemis Company, Inc., completed June 11, 2019 (FY2019) for $5.2B in an all-stock transaction; FY2021 activity was divestitures (a European hospital supplies business, businesses in India and Argentina, and the AMVIG stake). Justification: these are the acquisitions the 10-K acquisition notes and the 8-K disclose for each year.

Amcor primarily operates in the packaging industry: it is a global leader in developing and producing responsible packaging (flexible packaging, rigid containers, specialty cartons and closures) for food, beverage, pharmaceutical, medical, home and personal-care, and other consumer goods end markets, organized into two segments, Flexibles and Rigid Packaging. The FY2023 10-K describes this in both Item 1 and Note 1.

No. Amcor's FY2023 gross margin declined: gross profit fell to $2,725M from $2,820M, and gross margin dropped to 18.5% from 19.4% (about -90 bps). The filing attributes the decline mainly to the pass-through of higher raw material costs and the impact of disposed operations, and it notes the percentage is distorted by that pass-through, so gross margin is a weak signal for a packaging company like Amcor. Operating margin did rise (8.5% to 10.3%), but the filing attributes the net income increase mainly to the $215M Russian disposal gain and lower restructuring, not to gross profit.

Amcor's restructuring liability at December 31, 2022 (end of Q2 FY2023) was $93 million, comprising $81M employee costs, $2M fixed-asset-related costs and $10M other costs, down from $118M at June 30, 2022. It is an accrual for unpaid restructuring-plan costs, mainly from restructuring related to the Russia-Ukraine conflict, with the majority expected to be paid within twelve months and recorded in other current and non-current liabilities.

Amcor's fiscal 2023 (twelve months ended June 30, 2023) Adjusted EBITDA was $2,018 million, down from $2,117 million in fiscal 2022 (about -5%). The company's reconciliation table starts from reported EBITDA of $2,080 million and adds back items such as Russia-Ukraine conflict impacts (-$90m), hyperinflation, and interest-related items to reach $2,018m. Adjusted EBIT was $1,608m and Adjusted EPS was 73.3 cents.

Real (comparable constant-currency) net sales growth for FY2023 vs FY2022 was 0%, i.e. flat. Reported growth was 1% (14,694 vs 14,544 $M). Removing FX (about -3 pts), raw-material pass-through (about +5 pts) and items affecting comparability (about -1 pt) gives 1 + 3 - 5 + 1 = 0%. The company's own commentary says comparable constant-currency sales were 'in line with the prior year'.

FY2015 D&A margin is about 4.18%: D&A of $167M from the cash flow statement divided by net revenue of $3,991M from the income statement (167 / 3,991 = 4.18%). Net revenue is from the Consolidated Statements of Operations and D&A is the 'Depreciation and amortization' add-back in operating cash flows, both for the year ended December 26, 2015.

Yes. AMD's FY22 quick ratio is about 1.57x: (cash $4,835M + short-term investments $1,020M + accounts receivable $4,126M) / total current liabilities $6,369M = $9,981M / $6,369M. A quick ratio above 1.0x means liquid assets cover current liabilities without selling inventory, which is the relevant test here because inventories rose to $3,771M and the current ratio of 2.36x (current assets $15,019M / $6,369M) depends on that inventory. The FY21 quick ratio was about 1.49x (($2,535M + $1,073M + $2,706M) / $4,240M), so liquidity was stable to slightly stronger year over year.

As of FY22, AMD sells high-performance and adaptive computing products organized into four reportable segments: Data Center (server CPUs and GPUs, DPUs, FPGAs and Adaptive SoCs for data centers), Client (CPUs, APUs and chipsets for desktop and notebook PCs), Gaming (discrete GPUs, semi-custom SoC products and development services), and Embedded (embedded CPUs, GPUs, APUs, FPGAs and Adaptive SoCs). The FPGA/Adaptive SoC line came from the Xilinx acquisition (Feb 2022) and the DPU line from Pensando (May 2022). AMD also sells or licenses portions of its IP from time to time. Justification: the FY22 10-K's Item 1 lists these four segments and their product lines.

FY22 (AMD 2022 10-K) net revenue rose 44% to $23.6B from $16.4B in 2021. The increase was driven by Data Center (+64% to $6.0B, on higher EPYC server processor sales), Gaming (+21% to $6.8B, on higher semi-custom sales), and Embedded (from $246M to $4.6B, mainly from including Xilinx embedded products after the February 2022 acquisition). Client revenue fell 10% to $6.2B on a weak PC market, partly offsetting these gains.

Operating margin fell from about 22.2% in FY21 to about 5.4% in FY22, a drop of roughly 17 percentage points. The main driver was about $3.5B of acquisition-related intangible amortization from the Xilinx deal ($1,448M in cost of sales plus $2,100M in operating expenses), which had no FY21 equivalent. Higher R&D ($5,005M vs $2,845M) and MG&A ($2,336M vs $1,448M) also pushed the margin down, partly offset by revenue growth to $23.6B. Computed from the statement table: operating income = gross profit − R&D − MG&A − amortization + licensing gain = $1,264M (FY22) vs $3,648M (FY21). Operating margin is still a useful metric for AMD, but the FY22 figure is distorted by the one-time acquisition amortization. Excluding that amortization, FY22 margin is about 20.4%, close to FY21's 22.2%.

Operations. In FY2022 (year ended Dec 31, 2022), net cash provided by operating activities was $3,565M, versus $1,999M provided by investing and $(3,264)M used in financing. Operations brought in the most cash and was the only one of the three that was a source of cash, so it has the largest positive cash flow.

Data Center. Excluding Embedded, FY21 to FY22 net revenue rose from $3,694M to $6,043M, up about 63.6%, versus Gaming up about 21.4% ($5,607M to $6,805M) and Client down about 10.0% ($6,887M to $6,201M). Data Center also had the largest dollar increase (+$2,349M).

Yes. AMD reported customer concentration for FY22: one customer accounted for 16% of consolidated net revenue for the year ended December 31, 2022 (sales from the Gaming segment), and the filing says losing this customer would have a material adverse effect. The 10-K also notes that one customer was about 18% of consolidated accounts receivable at December 31, 2022.

None. In American Express' 2022 10-K, the only security registered under Section 12(b) is the Common Shares (par value $0.20, symbol AXP) on the New York Stock Exchange. The cover page states "Securities registered pursuant to section 12(g) of the Act: None." No debt securities are listed as exchange-registered; the company's long-term debt is not shown as exchange-listed in these filings.

As of 2022, American Express's operations are organized into four geographic regions: United States, EMEA (Europe, Middle East and Africa), APAC (Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand), and LACC (Latin America, Canada and the Caribbean). The United States is the dominant region, with $41,396M of $52,862M total revenues net of interest expense (about 78%) and $10,383M of $9,585M consolidated pretax income before Other Unallocated costs. The 10-K's risk factors note that about 22% of 2022 revenues came from outside the United States, which is consistent with the regional split.

No. On the closest available proxy, pretax income over total revenues net of interest expense, AMEX's margin fell in 2022: 18.1% ($9,585M / $52,862M) versus 25.2% in 2021 ($10,689M / $42,380M), though it recovered from 11.9% in 2020. The drop is driven by provisions for credit losses swinging from a $1,419M release in 2021 to a $2,182M charge in 2022. Before provisions, the margin edged up from 21.9% to 22.3% ((revenues net of interest expense less total expenses) / revenues). The 10-K reports no operating income line, so 'operating margin' is not a metric the filing defines. For a card issuer and lender whose interest expense and credit provisions are core operating costs, the pretax margin on revenue net of interest expense is the most sensible substitute, and these ratios are my calculations from the reported figures.

Gross margin is not a useful metric here and is not reported. American Express's 10-K has no revenue-less-cost-of-sales line, so there is no gross margin to explain. Its FY2022 income statement shows total revenues net of interest expense of $52,862M (up 25% from $42,380M), driven mainly by Discount revenue (+25% to $30,739M). Total expenses rose to $41,095M, led by Card Member rewards ($14,002M vs $11,007M), and pretax income fell to $9,585M from $10,689M. The business is a payments network and lender whose main costs are rewards, business development, credit provisions and personnel, not cost of goods sold, so profit is better tracked through net revenue, the rewards-to-revenue ratio and pretax or net income.

American Express's effective tax rate fell by 3.0 percentage points, from 24.6% in FY2021 to 21.6% in FY2022. The MD&A attributes the decline primarily to discrete tax benefits in 2022 from resolving prior-year tax items.

Customer deposits were the largest liability at December 31, 2022, at $110,239 million, ahead of other liabilities ($37,350M), long-term debt ($42,573M), accounts payable ($12,133M) and short-term borrowings ($1,348M). Total liabilities were $203,643 million, so customer deposits were about 54% of that total.

Yes. American Express reported that Card Member retention remained high in 2022, alongside record new card acquisitions. Net card fees rose 17% year over year, which management attributed to those acquisitions and retention. Proprietary cards-in-force also grew from 71.4 million to 76.7 million (+7%), and billed business rose 23%.
About $0.389 billion (USD 389 million) in dividends paid in FY2020, per the "Dividends paid" line in the consolidated statement of cash flows (shown as (389) in millions, a cash outflow).

Unadjusted EBITDA for FY2021 is $1,832 million: operating income of $1,196 million from the income statement plus depreciation and amortization of $636 million from the cash flow statement (1,196 + 636 = 1,832). This follows the question's method of pairing the income statement's operating income with the cash flow statement's D&A, with no adjustments.

No. American Water Works had negative working capital at December 31, 2022: total current assets of $1,250M minus total current liabilities of $2,811M gives a deficit of about $1,561M. The 10-K's own risk factor states that working capital (current assets less current liabilities) was in a deficit position, which is consistent with the balance sheet.

2.8% — the FY2015–FY2017 average of annual net-profit margins (net earnings attributable to Best Buy ÷ revenue) is (3.06% + 2.27% + 3.12%) ÷ 3 ≈ 2.8%. FY2015 = $1,233M / $40,339M = 3.06%; FY2016 = $897M / $39,528M = 2.27%; FY2017 = $1,228M / $39,403M = 3.12%. The FY2017 10-K's Consolidated Statements of Earnings is the source, and its three fiscal-year columns are the ones used.

Best Buy's merchandise inventories at fiscal FY2019 year end (February 2, 2019) were $5,409 million, per the Consolidated Balance Sheets of the fiscal 2019 10-K (up from $5,209 million at February 3, 2018).

Yes, if "2%" is read as percentage points. Best Buy's consolidated gross profit rate ran 23.3% (FY2016), 24.0% (FY2017), 23.4% (FY2018), 23.2% (FY2019), 23.0% (FY2020), 22.4% (FY2021), 22.5% (FY2022) and 21.4% (FY2023). Every annual move was 1.1 percentage points or less, the largest being the 1.1-point drop in FY2023. The rate is a relevant metric for Best Buy, which reports it in its consolidated results. Read as a relative change, the FY2023 drop (about 4.9%) and the FY2017, FY2018 and FY2021 moves (about 2.5–3%) exceed 2%, so the answer depends on that reading.

FY2023 (ended Jan 28, 2023): no acquisitions are disclosed for fiscal 2023. The FY2023 10-K describes only the fiscal 2022 deals, Current Health ($389M net cash, Nov 2, 2021) and Yardbird Furniture ($79M, Nov 4, 2021). FY2022 (ended Jan 29, 2022): Current Health Ltd. ($389M, care-at-home technology) and Two Peaks, LLC d/b/a Yardbird Furniture ($79M, direct-to-consumer outdoor furniture). FY2021 (ended Jan 30, 2021): no fiscal 2021 acquisitions are disclosed; the acquisitions note covers only BioSensics ($20M, Aug 2019), Critical Signal Technologies ($125M, May 2019) and GreatCall ($787M, Oct 2018), which were fiscal 2019–2020 deals. Justification: each 10-K's acquisitions note lists the deals and their dates, and the FY2023 filing itself attributes Current Health and Yardbird to fiscal 2022.

Operations was the largest contributor in FY2023 at +$1,824M of cash provided; investing used $(962)M and financing used $(1,806)M. Operating activities brought in the most cash, and financing lost the most. Investing lost less than financing, so it ranks second on the "lost the least" reading.

Yes, cash fell in every company I could match. The question names no company, so I checked the library for companies with a FY2023 balance sheet and a Q2 FY2024 filing. Best Buy: cash and cash equivalents went from $1,874M (Jan 28, 2023) to $1,093M (Jul 29, 2023), a drop of $781M (-41.7%). Salesforce: cash went from $7,016M (Jan 31, 2023) to $6,772M (Jul 31, 2023), a drop of $244M (-3.5%). Ulta Beauty's file labeled 2024Q2 actually reports fiscal 2023 Q2 (cash $388.6M) against a 10-K balance of $737.9M (Jan 28, 2023), a drop of $349.3M, so it is likely a mislabel and not a true FY2024 Q2 match. Best Buy is the most direct match by labels; please confirm which company you meant.

Yes, but only for Best Buy-branded domestic stores. The count fell from 925 at the end of fiscal 2023 to 907 at the end of Q2 FY2024, a net decrease of 18. Q1 FY2024 closings (925 to 908) and Q2 closings (1 store) account for the drop. Across the domestic segment, total stores went from 978 to 969. Canada Best Buy stores were flat at 160 in Q2 FY2024 versus 160 at Q2 FY2023, with one new store opened in Q2 FY2024. The 10-Q also says the company expects to close 20 to 30 Best Buy stores in fiscal 2024.

Computing and Mobile Phones was the top Domestic (USA) category in Q2 FY2024 (quarter ended July 29, 2023), with $3,674M of revenue, ahead of Consumer Electronics at $2,658M. It is the largest category in the Domestic segment, at 41% of Domestic revenue.

Working capital ratio ≈ 1.73. FY2016 total current assets of $1,001,425K divided by total current liabilities of $577,464K = 1.734, rounded to 1.73 (Square, Inc. consolidated balance sheet, December 31, 2016; the filing is titled Square, which is Block's former name).

Total net revenue grew from $4,713,500K in FY2019 to $9,497,578K in FY2020, a growth rate of (9,497,578 / 4,713,500) − 1 = 101.5%. This uses only the Consolidated Statement of Operations' total net revenue line, which includes the large jump in bitcoin revenue (from $516,465K to $4,571,543K).

Block (then Square, Inc.) generated $381.6 million of net cash provided by operating activities in FY2020 (381,603 thousand USD, as reported in the consolidated statement of cash flows; the same figure appears in the MD&A cash flow table). This is taken directly from the statement's 'Net cash provided by operating activities' line, so no calculation was needed.

Boeing's net property, plant and equipment at December 31, 2018 was $12,645 million, as reported directly on the Consolidated Statements of Financial Position (the balance sheet line 'Property, plant and equipment, net').

Yes, at the reportable-segment level. Of FY2022 total revenue of $66,608M, Commercial Airplanes (BCA) was $25,867M (38.8%), Defense, Space & Security (BDS) was $23,162M (34.8%), and Global Services (BGS) was $17,611M (26.4%). Each exceeds the 20% threshold of about $13,322M. Within the sub-categories disclosed in the sections read, none exceeds 20%: BGS Commercial was $9,560M (14.4%) and BGS Government was $7,681M (11.5%). Boeing Capital ($199M, 0.3%) and unallocated items do not exceed 20%. The 10-K sections read do not break out product-line revenue (e.g., 737 vs. 787), so that level was not tested.

Yes, in part. Boeing's FY2022 10-K reports ongoing matters but says it expects none to be material: the company describes "various legal proceedings" and says the outcome of pending matters "will not have a material effect" on financial position, results or cash flows. The notable matters are the 737 MAX/Lion Air and Ethiopian Airlines accident lawsuits (no reasonable estimate of loss not covered by insurance), and the Embraer arbitration over the terminated joint ventures (no reasonable estimate of loss). In 2022 Boeing also received $219 from a shareholder derivative settlement and paid a $200 SEC civil penalty. The 10-K itself flags litigation as a material risk factor, so the "not material" conclusion is management's stated view, not a guarantee.

Only marginally, and the metric is of limited use for Boeing. Boeing reports no gross profit line. Deriving it as total revenues less cost of products and cost of services gives $3,530M on $66,608M revenue in 2022 (5.3%), versus $3,049M on $62,286M (4.9%) in 2021 and a loss of -$5,642M (-9.7%) in 2020, so the derived margin rose about 40 bp. Gross margin is a poor guide here because cost of sales is recognized under program accounting for commercial aircraft and long-term contracts, so it swings with large earnings charges. The 2022 increase came mainly from higher revenue, while cost of sales still included charges at BDS, and the 10-K says cost of sales as a percentage of revenue was 'largely consistent' year over year (94.7% vs 95.2%).

Boeing's primary customers in FY2022 were commercial airlines and the U.S. government. The commercial airline industry worldwide is the customer base for the Commercial Airplanes segment (BCA), and the U.S. government accounted for 40% of 2022 consolidated revenues (vs. 49% in 2021 and 51% in 2020), mainly through BDS and BGS. Revenue by customer location was $39,218M from the United States and $27,374M from non-U.S. customers, of which Asia was $8,393M. The filing identifies airlines and the U.S. government as the principal customer groups, though it does not rank them in a single list.

Yes. Boeing's 10-K (FY2017) states that "Traditionally, the airline industry has been cyclical and very competitive and has experienced significant profit swings," and that demand for its commercial aircraft is shaped by airline profitability, financing availability, and fuel prices. The same risk-factor language recurs in the FY2015–FY2022 10-Ks, and the FY2015 and FY2017 MD&A notes that the cyclicality of its commercial and defense markets sometimes offset each other.

Boeing's FY2022 10-K (the latest filing in the library before FY2023) forecasts these FY2023 production changes: 737 — further gradual rate increases from the current 31 per month, based on market demand and supply chain capacity (no specific target given); 787 — gradual return from low rates to 5 per month in 2023; 777X-9 — production paused during 2022 and 2023, with roughly $1.5 billion of abnormal costs expected until production resumes. The 767 (3/month) and 777/777X (3/month combined) are described as current rates with no stated FY2023 change. Yes. CVS Health's 10-Ks for 2020, 2021 and 2022 each disclose ongoing material litigation. Yes. At Dec 31, 2022, PayPal's working capital was positive at $12,416M (total current assets $57,517M minus total current liabilities $45,101M). Not on the quick ratio alone. Verizon's FY2022 quick ratio is about 0.54x: (cash $2,605M + accounts receivable, net $24,506M) / total current liabilities $50,171M = $27,111M / $50,171M. That is well below the 1.0x benchmark, so the balance sheet has no cushion to meet current obligations from liquid assets. The quick ratio is still relevant for Verizon, but it is conservative: it excludes $2,388M of inventory and $8,358M of prepaid expenses, and the 10-K says sources from operations and external financing are sufficient for the next 12 months and beyond. Liquidity looks adequate on those cash-generation and financing grounds, but the quick ratio itself does not show a healthy position. No current marketable securities are reported; debt securities sit in other assets.
